title: Alleviating non-radiative losses in organic solar cells through side-chain regulation of low-bandgap non-fullerene acceptors

paper_content.abstract: Non-radiative losses present a significant hurdle limiting the performance of organic solar cells (OSCs). Selenium substitution in non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) is an effective approach for tuning intermolecular stacking and energy levels in state-of-the-art near-infrared absorbing OSCs. However, the inter-system crossing (ISC) induced by selenium may enhance the formation of triplet excitons in NFAs, aggravating non-radiative losses in OSCs. Herein, we have structurally engineered selenium-containing NFAs through introducing achiral N-alkyl substituents with varied branching sites at C2 or C3 position onto the pyrrole moiety of NFA core. We find that the C2-branched ones in our material system exhibit more intimate molecular packing, improved luminescence efficiency and reduced triplet exciton generation in both neat and blend films, reflected as improved external quantum efficiencies and open-circuit voltages in higher-performance devices. We utilize the best-performing NFA as a ternary component into the benchmark D18:L8-BO absorber to realize a high efficiency of 20.4% (certified as 19.88%). This work shows how precisely regulating the microstructure of NFAs by side-chain modification can reduce the non-radiative losses of OSCs.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript entitled “Alleviating non-radiative losses in organic solar cells through side-chain regulation of low-bandgap non-fullerene acceptors” presents a systematic investigation of how N-alkyl side-chain steric in Se-substituted non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) influence molecular packing, excited-state dynamics, and ultimately photovoltaic performance. In this work, Qi et al. designed and synthesized a series of NFAs (S9SHO-F, S9SBH-F, S9SHN-F and S9S3B-F) bearing different alkyl side-chains. Through single-crystal X-ray diffraction, device-physics analysis and morphology characterization, they found that larger steric hindrance contributes to a reduction in intersystem crossing (ISC) to triplet excitons (T₁) and suppresses non-radiative loss, which in turn improves photovoltage and efficiency. However, several issues need to be addressed before publication.
> In this manuscript, Qi et al. claim that NFAs with bulkier side-chains exhibit more intimate molecular packing, which contradicts previous reports. Li et al. observed that the π–π stacking d-spacing increases gradually as the branched alkyl chain length increases (Nat. Energy 2021, 6, 605-613). Moreover, reducing steric interactions between the core and the branches has been shown to strengthen π–π stacking (Joule 2019, 3, 3020-3033; Chem. Rev. 2022, 122, 14180−14274; Nat. Mater. 2025, 24, 433-443). I suggest that the authors provide more convincing evidence to rationalize their observations, which would enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript.
> The NFA, S9SHO-F, with more sterically hindered substituents exhibits the more compact stacking and the highest luminescence efficiency among the four NFAs. Considering that organic photovoltaic materials typically follow the aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) principle, stronger aggregation is generally expected to reduce luminescence efficiency. However, the trend reported in this work is the opposite. Could the authors provide a reasonable explanation for this apparent contradiction?
> In this work, the authors attribute the suppressed formation of T₁ to a steric-hindrance-induced reduction in ISC. However, the involvement of ISC in T₁ generation remains questionable because heavy-atom-free analogues were not investigated. Therefore, I recommend that the authors prepare and characterize Se-free control NFAs to clarify the origin of T₁ states and the associated energy losses. Such a comparison would greatly aid readers in distinguishing heavy-atom-mediated ISC from other possible pathways (e.g., charge-transfer-mediated triplet formation or geminate recombination).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors synthesized high-performance acceptor materials with near-infrared absorption properties via substitution with three selenophenes. Further studies revealed that alkyl substituents with greater steric hindrance can induce the formation of tight and ordered molecular packing and suppress non-radiative energy loss. Eventually, the binary and ternary devices based on D18:S9SHO-F achieved high efficiencies of 19.2% and 20.4% respectively, which provides significant reference for the design and synthesis of narrow-bandgap acceptor materials with low energy loss. Therefore, I suggest that the manuscript can be published in Nature Communications after minor revisions.
Some comments and suggestions are following:
(1) The performance of the D18:S9SHO-F -based binary and ternary devices in this paper is excellent, the author needs to provide the stability test data.
(2) The authors need to analyze the reasons for the performance improvement of D18:L8-BO:S9SHO-F based ternary devices, including aspects of morphology and exciton dynamics.
(3) In describing the increase in CCL observed in the GIWAXS of the blend films, the authors infer that “indicating a better morphology compatibility between S9SHO-F and D18”. It is necessary to conduct thin film surface contact angle experiments to verify the compatibility between the donor and acceptor.
(4) Generally, side chains with larger steric hindrance tend to hinder molecular packing, which is not conducive to the formation of a tight and ordered packing network. In this paper, how do the starting position of the branched chains and the length of the branched chains affect molecular packing? The author needs to carefully analyze the molecular single crystal structure.
(5) In most cases, selenium atom substitution results in the red shift of absorption, however, the inferior PCEs (FFs) comparing to their sulfur counterparts, especially for 5Se acceptor with 5-selenium substitution. What is the inner reason for that?
(6) Some format suggestions: for abbreviations that appear for the first time in the article, their corresponding English full names should be listed, such as the abbreviation of “GIWAXS”. It is suggested that the authors carefully check the entire text.

Response to the Reviewer 1
1. In this manuscript, Qi et al. claim that NFAs with bulkier side-chains exhibit more intimate molecular
packing, which contradicts previous reports. Li et al. observed that the π–π stacking d-spacing
increases gradually as the branched alkyl chain length increases (Nat. Energy 2021, 6, 605-613).
Moreover, reducing steric interactions between the core and the branches has been shown to strengthen
π–π stacking (Joule 2019, 3, 3020-3033; Chem. Rev. 2022, 122, 14180−14274; Nat. Mater. 2025, 24,
433-443). I suggest that the authors provide more convincing evidence to rationalize their observations,
which would enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer for the insightful comment. For the reported NFAs (Nat. Energy
2021, 6, 605-613), the authors engineered the branching alkyl chains flanking outward the NFA core,
giving a closer π–π distance in L8-BO (3.19 Å) when comparing with L8-HD (3.30 Å) and L8-OD (3.40
Å). In our work, we focus on the regulation of the branching position of N-alkyl chains on the pyrrole
unit, which locate at the inner side of the molecule. It is notable that in our previous works, we observed
from the single crystals of NFAs that the size of N-alkyl chains may not necessarily affect the value of
π–π distance. For example, the π–π distance of Y6 (N-2-ethylhexyl, 3.3-3.6 Å, ref: J. Am. Chem. Soc.
2020, 142, 15246-15251) is close to that of T9TBO-F (N-2-butyloctyl, 3.3-3.5 Å, ref: Nat. Energy 2022,
7, 1076-1086). This should be attributed to the complicated intermolecular interactions of NFA
molecules in condensed phase, and there are factors beyond the size of N-alkyl chains that may affect
molecular packing. To better explain how the steric effect of N-alkyl substituents affects the molecular
packing in our materials and gain clarity to the readers, we have analyzed the single-crystal data of
NFAs in a more in-depth manner and provided detailed explanations. We have also made modifications
to relevant statements to clarify this.
From the single-crystal analysis, S9SBH-F with the shortest N-alkyl chain forms an ordered 3D
honeycomb network, similar to the previously reported Y6 (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2020, 142, 15246-15251).
Compared with S9SBH-F, S9SHO-F with longer branched N-alkyl chains exhibits a long-range ordered
packing in the oblique direction across the crystal lattice (Supplementary Fig. 11), forming columns
composed of π-stacked NFA molecules with a small average π-π stacking distance (3.38 Å for S9SBH-
F, and 3.20 Å for S9SHO-F). The transition of crystal packing structure from a 3D honeycomb network
(S9SBH-F) into a network of rather independent columns (S9SHO-F) is caused by the long N-alkyl
chains occupying the interval between the adjacent columns in S9SHO-F single crystal, and results in
a mismatch between the two parallel molecules. When changing the branching site from C2-position to
C3-position, although the branching site of N-alkyls moves farther from the π-system, they still occupy
the interval between the adjacent molecular columns thus the packing patterns of S9S3B-F and S9SHN-
F are similar to that of S9SHO-F (Supplementary Fig. 12). We also infer that the distance between the
neighboring columns, which is associated with the size of N-alkyl substituents, may offer the flexibility
for NFA molecules to pack in a tighter manner. Therefore, we observe a reverse trend between the
distance in the neighboring columns (10.8 Å < 15.3 Å < 19.5 Å) and π-π stacking distance (3.52 Å >
3.50 Å > 3.20 Å) in S9S3B-F, S9SHN-F, and S9SHO-F (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 6).
To further investigate the π-π stacking in the neat NFAs, we conducted grazing-incidence wide-angle
X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) measurement of the C2-position and C3-position acceptors. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. 13, S9SHO-F shows a (010) diffraction peak at 1.76 Å-1 corresponding with a d-
spacing of 3.57 Å in the out-of-plane (OOP) direction. When changing the branching site to C3-position,
S9SHN-F exhibits a (010) diffraction peak at 1.73 Å-1 with a d-spacing of 3.63 Å in the OOP direction,
indicating a slightly more intimate packing in C2-position acceptor. These results are consistent with
our conclusions obtained from the single crystal analysis.

The manuscript entitled “Alleviating non-radiative losses in organic solar cells through side-chain regulation of low-bandgap non-fullerene acceptors” presents a systematic investigation of how N-alkyl side-chain steric in Se-substituted non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) influence molecular packing, excited-state dynamics, and ultimately photovoltaic performance. In this work, Qi et al. designed and synthesized a series of NFAs (S9SHO-F, S9SBH-F, S9SHN-F and S9S3B-F) bearing different alkyl side-chains. Through single-crystal X-ray diffraction, device-physics analysis and morphology characterization, they found that larger steric hindrance contributes to a reduction in intersystem crossing (ISC) to triplet excitons (T₁) and suppresses non-radiative loss, which in turn improves photovoltage and efficiency. However, several issues need to be addressed before publication.
> In this manuscript, Qi et al. claim that NFAs with bulkier side-chains exhibit more intimate molecular packing, which contradicts previous reports. Li et al. observed that the π–π stacking d-spacing increases gradually as the branched alkyl chain length increases (Nat. Energy 2021, 6, 605-613). Moreover, reducing steric interactions between the core and the branches has been shown to strengthen π–π stacking (Joule 2019, 3, 3020-3033; Chem. Rev. 2022, 122, 14180−14274; Nat. Mater. 2025, 24, 433-443). I suggest that the authors provide more convincing evidence to rationalize their observations, which would enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript.
> The NFA, S9SHO-F, with more sterically hindered substituents exhibits the more compact stacking and the highest luminescence efficiency among the four NFAs. Considering that organic photovoltaic materials typically follow the aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) principle, stronger aggregation is generally expected to reduce luminescence efficiency. However, the trend reported in this work is the opposite. Could the authors provide a reasonable explanation for this apparent contradiction?
> In this work, the authors attribute the suppressed formation of T₁ to a steric-hindrance-induced reduction in ISC. However, the involvement of ISC in T₁ generation remains questionable because heavy-atom-free analogues were not investigated. Therefore, I recommend that the authors prepare and characterize Se-free control NFAs to clarify the origin of T₁ states and the associated energy losses. Such a comparison would greatly aid readers in distinguishing heavy-atom-mediated ISC from other possible pathways (e.g., charge-transfer-mediated triplet formation or geminate recombination).

### Reviewer 2

The authors synthesized high-performance acceptor materials with near-infrared absorption properties via substitution with three selenophenes. Further studies revealed that alkyl substituents with greater steric hindrance can induce the formation of tight and ordered molecular packing and suppress non-radiative energy loss. Eventually, the binary and ternary devices based on D18:S9SHO-F achieved high efficiencies of 19.2% and 20.4% respectively, which provides significant reference for the design and synthesis of narrow-bandgap acceptor materials with low energy loss. Therefore, I suggest that the manuscript can be published in Nature Communications after minor revisions.
Some comments and suggestions are following:
(1) The performance of the D18:S9SHO-F -based binary and ternary devices in this paper is excellent, the author needs to provide the stability test data.
(2) The authors need to analyze the reasons for the performance improvement of D18:L8-BO:S9SHO-F based ternary devices, including aspects of morphology and exciton dynamics.
(3) In describing the increase in CCL observed in the GIWAXS of the blend films, the authors infer that “indicating a better morphology compatibility between S9SHO-F and D18”. It is necessary to conduct thin film surface contact angle experiments to verify the compatibility between the donor and acceptor.
(4) Generally, side chains with larger steric hindrance tend to hinder molecular packing, which is not conducive to the formation of a tight and ordered packing network. In this paper, how do the starting position of the branched chains and the length of the branched chains affect molecular packing? The author needs to carefully analyze the molecular single crystal structure.
(5) In most cases, selenium atom substitution results in the red shift of absorption, however, the inferior PCEs (FFs) comparing to their sulfur counterparts, especially for 5Se acceptor with 5-selenium substitution. What is the inner reason for that?
(6) Some format suggestions: for abbreviations that appear for the first time in the article, their corresponding English full names should be listed, such as the abbreviation of “GIWAXS”. It is suggested that the authors carefully check the entire text.

## Abstract

Non-radiative losses present a significant hurdle limiting the performance of organic solar cells (OSCs). Selenium substitution in non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) is an effective approach for tuning intermolecular stacking and energy levels in state-of-the-art near-infrared absorbing OSCs. However, the inter-system crossing (ISC) induced by selenium may enhance the formation of triplet excitons in NFAs, aggravating non-radiative losses in OSCs. Herein, we have structurally engineered selenium-containing NFAs through introducing achiral N-alkyl substituents with varied branching sites at C2 or C3 position onto the pyrrole moiety of NFA core. We find that the C2-branched ones in our material system exhibit more intimate molecular packing, improved luminescence efficiency and reduced triplet exciton generation in both neat and blend films, reflected as improved external quantum efficiencies and open-circuit voltages in higher-performance devices. We utilize the best-performing NFA as a ternary component into the benchmark D18:L8-BO absorber to realize a high efficiency of 20.4% (certified as 19.88%). ### Reviewer 1

The manuscript entitled “Alleviating non-radiative losses in organic solar cells through side-chain regulation of low-bandgap non-fullerene acceptors” presents a systematic investigation of how N-alkyl side-chain steric in Se-substituted non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) influence molecular packing, excited-state dynamics, and ultimately photovoltaic performance. In this work, Qi et al. designed and synthesized a series of NFAs (S9SHO-F, S9SBH-F, S9SHN-F and S9S3B-F) bearing different alkyl side-chains. Through single-crystal X-ray diffraction, device-physics analysis and morphology characterization, they found that larger steric hindrance contributes to a reduction in intersystem crossing (ISC) to triplet excitons (T₁) and suppresses non-radiative loss, which in turn improves photovoltage and efficiency. However, several issues need to be addressed before publication.
> In this manuscript, Qi et al. claim that NFAs with bulkier side-chains exhibit more intimate molecular packing, which contradicts previous reports. Li et al. observed that the π–π stacking d-spacing increases gradually as the branched alkyl chain length increases (Nat. Energy 2021, 6, 605-613). Moreover, reducing steric interactions between the core and the branches has been shown to strengthen π–π stacking (Joule 2019, 3, 3020-3033; Chem. Rev. 2022, 122, 14180−14274; Nat. Mater. 2025, 24, 433-443). I suggest that the authors provide more convincing evidence to rationalize their observations, which would enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript.
> The NFA, S9SHO-F, with more sterically hindered substituents exhibits the more compact stacking and the highest luminescence efficiency among the four NFAs. Considering that organic photovoltaic materials typically follow the aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) principle, stronger aggregation is generally expected to reduce luminescence efficiency. However, the trend reported in this work is the opposite. Could the authors provide a reasonable explanation for this apparent contradiction?
> In this work, the authors attribute the suppressed formation of T₁ to a steric-hindrance-induced reduction in ISC. However, the involvement of ISC in T₁ generation remains questionable because heavy-atom-free analogues were not investigated. Therefore, I recommend that the authors prepare and characterize Se-free control NFAs to clarify the origin of T₁ states and the associated energy losses. Such a comparison would greatly aid readers in distinguishing heavy-atom-mediated ISC from other possible pathways (e.g., charge-transfer-mediated triplet formation or geminate recombination).

Response to the Reviewer 1
1. In this manuscript, Qi et al. claim that NFAs with bulkier side-chains exhibit more intimate molecular
packing, which contradicts previous reports. Li et al. observed that the π–π stacking d-spacing
increases gradually as the branched alkyl chain length increases (Nat. Energy 2021, 6, 605-613).
Moreover, reducing steric interactions between the core and the branches has been shown to strengthen
π–π stacking (Joule 2019, 3, 3020-3033; Chem. Rev. 2022, 122, 14180−14274; Nat. Mater. 2025, 24,
433-443). I suggest that the authors provide more convincing evidence to rationalize their observations,
which would enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer for the insightful comment. For the reported NFAs (Nat. Energy
2021, 6, 605-613), the authors engineered the branching alkyl chains flanking outward the NFA core,
giving a closer π–π distance in L8-BO (3.19 Å) when comparing with L8-HD (3.30 Å) and L8-OD (3.40
Å). In our work, we focus on the regulation of the branching position of N-alkyl chains on the pyrrole
unit, which locate at the inner side of the molecule. It is notable that in our previous works, we observed
from the single crystals of NFAs that the size of N-alkyl chains may not necessarily affect the value of
π–π distance. For example, the π–π distance of Y6 (N-2-ethylhexyl, 3.3-3.6 Å, ref: J. Am. Chem. Soc.
2020, 142, 15246-15251) is close to that of T9TBO-F (N-2-butyloctyl, 3.3-3.5 Å, ref: Nat. Energy 2022,
7, 1076-1086). This should be attributed to the complicated intermolecular interactions of NFA
molecules in condensed phase, and there are factors beyond the size of N-alkyl chains that may affect
molecular packing. To better explain how the steric effect of N-alkyl substituents affects the molecular
packing in our materials and gain clarity to the readers, we have analyzed the single-crystal data of
NFAs in a more in-depth manner and provided detailed explanations. We have also made modifications
to relevant statements to clarify this.
From the single-crystal analysis, S9SBH-F with the shortest N-alkyl chain forms an ordered 3D
honeycomb network, similar to the previously reported Y6 (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2020, 142, 15246-15251).
Compared with S9SBH-F, S9SHO-F with longer branched N-alkyl chains exhibits a long-range ordered
packing in the oblique direction across the crystal lattice (Supplementary Fig. 11), forming columns
composed of π-stacked NFA molecules with a small average π-π stacking distance (3.38 Å for S9SBH-
F, and 3.20 Å for S9SHO-F). The transition of crystal packing structure from a 3D honeycomb network
(S9SBH-F) into a network of rather independent columns (S9SHO-F) is caused by the long N-alkyl
chains occupying the interval between the adjacent columns in S9SHO-F single crystal, and results in
a mismatch between the two parallel molecules. When changing the branching site from C2-position to
C3-position, although the branching site of N-alkyls moves farther from the π-system, they still occupy
the interval between the adjacent molecular columns thus the packing patterns of S9S3B-F and S9SHN-
F are similar to that of S9SHO-F (Supplementary Fig. 12). We also infer that the distance between the
neighboring columns, which is associated with the size of N-alkyl substituents, may offer the flexibility
for NFA molecules to pack in a tighter manner. Therefore, we observe a reverse trend between the
distance in the neighboring columns (10.8 Å < 15.3 Å < 19.5 Å) and π-π stacking distance (3.52 Å >
3.50 Å > 3.20 Å) in S9S3B-F, S9SHN-F, and S9SHO-F (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 6).
To further investigate the π-π stacking in the neat NFAs, we conducted grazing-incidence wide-angle
X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) measurement of the C2-position and C3-position acceptors. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. 13, S9SHO-F shows a (010) diffraction peak at 1.76 Å-1 corresponding with a d-
spacing of 3.57 Å in the out-of-plane (OOP) direction. When changing the branching site to C3-position,
S9SHN-F exhibits a (010) diffraction peak at 1.73 Å-1 with a d-spacing of 3.63 Å in the OOP direction,
indicating a slightly more intimate packing in C2-position acceptor. These results are consistent with
our conclusions obtained from the single crystal analysis.

4. Generally, side chains with larger steric hindrance tend to hinder molecular packing, which is not
conducive to the formation of a tight and ordered packing network. In this paper, how do the starting
position of the branched chains and the length of the branched chains affect molecular packing? The
author needs to carefully analyze the molecular single crystal structure.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer for the insightful comment. To better explain how side-chain steric
hindrance affects the molecular packing in our work, we have analyzed the single-crystal data of NFAs
in a more in-depth manner and provided detailed explanations.
From the single-crystal analysis, S9SBH-F with the shortest N-alkyl chain forms an ordered 3D
honeycomb network, similar to the previously reported Y6 (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2020, 142, 15246-15251).
Compared with S9SBH-F, S9SHO-F with longer branched N-alkyl chains exhibits a long-range ordered
packing in the oblique direction across the crystal lattice (Supplementary Fig. 11), forming columns
composed of π-stacked NFA molecules with a small average π-π stacking distance (3.38 Å for S9SBH-
F, and 3.20 Å for S9SHO-F). The transition of crystal packing structure from a 3D honeycomb network
(S9SBH-F) into a network of rather independent columns (S9SHO-F) is caused by the long N-alkyl
chains occupying the interval between the adjacent columns in S9SHO-F single crystal, and results in
a mismatch between the two parallel molecules. When changing the branching site from C2-position to
C3-position, although the branching site of N-alkyls moves farther from the π-system, they still occupy
the interval between the adjacent molecular columns thus the packing patterns of S9S3B-F and S9SHN-
F are similar to that of S9SHO-F (Supplementary Fig. 12). We also infer that the distance between the
neighboring columns, which is associated with the size of N-alkyl substituents, may offer the flexibility
for NFA molecules to pack in a tighter manner. Therefore, we observe a reverse trend between the
distance in the neighboring columns (10.8 Å < 15.3 Å < 19.5 Å) and π-π stacking distance (3.52 Å >
3.50 Å > 3.20 Å) in S9S3B-F, S9SHN-F, and S9SHO-F (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 6).
To further investigate the π-π stacking in the neat NFAs, we conducted grazing-incidence wide-angle
X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) measurement of the C2-position and C3-position acceptors. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. 13, S9SHO-F shows a (010) diffraction peak at 1.76 Å-1 corresponding with a d-
spacing of 3.57 Å in the out-of-plane (OOP) direction. When changing the branching site to C3-position,
S9SHN-F exhibits a (010) diffraction peak at 1.73 Å-1 with a d-spacing of 3.63 Å in the OOP direction,
indicating a slightly more intimate packing in C2-position acceptor. These results are consistent with
our conclusions obtained from the single crystal analysis.

5. In most cases, selenium atom substitution results in the red shift of absorption, however, the inferior
PCEs (FFs) comparing to their sulfur counterparts, especially for 5Se acceptor with 5-selenium
substitution. What is the inner reason for that?
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer for the insightful comment. Selenium is more polarizable than sulfur,
and the lone pairs on selenium facilitates stronger interatomic interactions between adjacent selenium
atoms, resulting in enhanced intermolecular Se⋯Se interactions (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2015, 137, 1314;
Acc. Chem. Res. 2021, 54, 3906; Sol. RRL 2022, 6, 2200156). When introducing 5 selenium to the
design of small-molecule acceptors, it may induce excessively strong intermolecular Se⋯Se
interactions, leading to over-aggregation of the acceptor phase and inadequate miscibility between the
donor and acceptor, resulting in a non-ideal morphology. Therefore, the generation and transport of
charge carrier could be prohibited and leads to an inferior FF, as well as PCE.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript entitled “Alleviating non-radiative losses in organic solar cells through side-chain regulation of low-bandgap non-fullerene acceptors” presents a systematic investigation of how N-alkyl side-chain steric in Se-substituted non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) influence molecular packing, excited-state dynamics, and ultimately photovoltaic performance. In this work, Qi et al. designed and synthesized a series of NFAs (S9SHO-F, S9SBH-F, S9SHN-F and S9S3B-F) bearing different alkyl side-chains. Through single-crystal X-ray diffraction, device-physics analysis and morphology characterization, they found that larger steric hindrance contributes to a reduction in intersystem crossing (ISC) to triplet excitons (T₁) and suppresses non-radiative loss, which in turn improves photovoltage and efficiency. However, several issues need to be addressed before publication.
> In this manuscript, Qi et al. claim that NFAs with bulkier side-chains exhibit more intimate molecular packing, which contradicts previous reports. Li et al. observed that the π–π stacking d-spacing increases gradually as the branched alkyl chain length increases (Nat. Energy 2021, 6, 605-613). Moreover, reducing steric interactions between the core and the branches has been shown to strengthen π–π stacking (Joule 2019, 3, 3020-3033; Chem. Rev. 2022, 122, 14180−14274; Nat. Mater. 2025, 24, 433-443). I suggest that the authors provide more convincing evidence to rationalize their observations, which would enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript.
> The NFA, S9SHO-F, with more sterically hindered substituents exhibits the more compact stacking and the highest luminescence efficiency among the four NFAs. Considering that organic photovoltaic materials typically follow the aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) principle, stronger aggregation is generally expected to reduce luminescence efficiency. However, the trend reported in this work is the opposite. Could the authors provide a reasonable explanation for this apparent contradiction?
> In this work, the authors attribute the suppressed formation of T₁ to a steric-hindrance-induced reduction in ISC. However, the involvement of ISC in T₁ generation remains questionable because heavy-atom-free analogues were not investigated. Therefore, I recommend that the authors prepare and characterize Se-free control NFAs to clarify the origin of T₁ states and the associated energy losses. Such a comparison would greatly aid readers in distinguishing heavy-atom-mediated ISC from other possible pathways (e.g., charge-transfer-mediated triplet formation or geminate recombination).

### Reviewer 2

The authors synthesized high-performance acceptor materials with near-infrared absorption properties via substitution with three selenophenes. Further studies revealed that alkyl substituents with greater steric hindrance can induce the formation of tight and ordered molecular packing and suppress non-radiative energy loss. Eventually, the binary and ternary devices based on D18:S9SHO-F achieved high efficiencies of 19.2% and 20.4% respectively, which provides significant reference for the design and synthesis of narrow-bandgap acceptor materials with low energy loss. Therefore, I suggest that the manuscript can be published in Nature Communications after minor revisions.
Some comments and suggestions are following:
(1) The performance of the D18:S9SHO-F -based binary and ternary devices in this paper is excellent, the author needs to provide the stability test data.
(2) The authors need to analyze the reasons for the performance improvement of D18:L8-BO:S9SHO-F based ternary devices, including aspects of morphology and exciton dynamics.
(3) In describing the increase in CCL observed in the GIWAXS of the blend films, the authors infer that “indicating a better morphology compatibility between S9SHO-F and D18”. It is necessary to conduct thin film surface contact angle experiments to verify the compatibility between the donor and acceptor.
(4) Generally, side chains with larger steric hindrance tend to hinder molecular packing, which is not conducive to the formation of a tight and ordered packing network. In this paper, how do the starting position of the branched chains and the length of the branched chains affect molecular packing? The author needs to carefully analyze the molecular single crystal structure.
(5) In most cases, selenium atom substitution results in the red shift of absorption, however, the inferior PCEs (FFs) comparing to their sulfur counterparts, especially for 5Se acceptor with 5-selenium substitution. What is the inner reason for that?
(6) Some format suggestions: for abbreviations that appear for the first time in the article, their corresponding English full names should be listed, such as the abbreviation of “GIWAXS”. It is suggested that the authors carefully check the entire text.

Response to the Reviewer 1
1. In this manuscript, Qi et al. claim that NFAs with bulkier side-chains exhibit more intimate molecular
packing, which contradicts previous reports. Li et al. observed that the π–π stacking d-spacing
increases gradually as the branched alkyl chain length increases (Nat. Energy 2021, 6, 605-613).
Moreover, reducing steric interactions between the core and the branches has been shown to strengthen
π–π stacking (Joule 2019, 3, 3020-3033; Chem. Rev. 2022, 122, 14180−14274; Nat. Mater. 2025, 24,
433-443). I suggest that the authors provide more convincing evidence to rationalize their observations,
which would enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer for the insightful comment. For the reported NFAs (Nat. Energy
2021, 6, 605-613), the authors engineered the branching alkyl chains flanking outward the NFA core,
giving a closer π–π distance in L8-BO (3.19 Å) when comparing with L8-HD (3.30 Å) and L8-OD (3.40
Å). In our work, we focus on the regulation of the branching position of N-alkyl chains on the pyrrole
unit, which locate at the inner side of the molecule. It is notable that in our previous works, we observed
from the single crystals of NFAs that the size of N-alkyl chains may not necessarily affect the value of
π–π distance. For example, the π–π distance of Y6 (N-2-ethylhexyl, 3.3-3.6 Å, ref: J. Am. Chem. Soc.
2020, 142, 15246-15251) is close to that of T9TBO-F (N-2-butyloctyl, 3.3-3.5 Å, ref: Nat. Energy 2022,
7, 1076-1086). This should be attributed to the complicated intermolecular interactions of NFA
molecules in condensed phase, and there are factors beyond the size of N-alkyl chains that may affect
molecular packing. To better explain how the steric effect of N-alkyl substituents affects the molecular
packing in our materials and gain clarity to the readers, we have analyzed the single-crystal data of
NFAs in a more in-depth manner and provided detailed explanations. We have also made modifications
to relevant statements to clarify this.
From the single-crystal analysis, S9SBH-F with the shortest N-alkyl chain forms an ordered 3D
honeycomb network, similar to the previously reported Y6 (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2020, 142, 15246-15251).
Compared with S9SBH-F, S9SHO-F with longer branched N-alkyl chains exhibits a long-range ordered
packing in the oblique direction across the crystal lattice (Supplementary Fig. 11), forming columns
composed of π-stacked NFA molecules with a small average π-π stacking distance (3.38 Å for S9SBH-
F, and 3.20 Å for S9SHO-F). The transition of crystal packing structure from a 3D honeycomb network
(S9SBH-F) into a network of rather independent columns (S9SHO-F) is caused by the long N-alkyl
chains occupying the interval between the adjacent columns in S9SHO-F single crystal, and results in
a mismatch between the two parallel molecules. When changing the branching site from C2-position to
C3-position, although the branching site of N-alkyls moves farther from the π-system, they still occupy
the interval between the adjacent molecular columns thus the packing patterns of S9S3B-F and S9SHN-
F are similar to that of S9SHO-F (Supplementary Fig. 12). We also infer that the distance between the
neighboring columns, which is associated with the size of N-alkyl substituents, may offer the flexibility
for NFA molecules to pack in a tighter manner. Therefore, we observe a reverse trend between the
distance in the neighboring columns (10.8 Å < 15.3 Å < 19.5 Å) and π-π stacking distance (3.52 Å >
3.50 Å > 3.20 Å) in S9S3B-F, S9SHN-F, and S9SHO-F (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 6).
To further investigate the π-π stacking in the neat NFAs, we conducted grazing-incidence wide-angle
X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) measurement of the C2-position and C3-position acceptors. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. 13, S9SHO-F shows a (010) diffraction peak at 1.76 Å-1 corresponding with a d-
spacing of 3.57 Å in the out-of-plane (OOP) direction. When changing the branching site to C3-position,
S9SHN-F exhibits a (010) diffraction peak at 1.73 Å-1 with a d-spacing of 3.63 Å in the OOP direction,
indicating a slightly more intimate packing in C2-position acceptor. These results are consistent with
our conclusions obtained from the single crystal analysis.

4. Generally, side chains with larger steric hindrance tend to hinder molecular packing, which is not
conducive to the formation of a tight and ordered packing network. In this paper, how do the starting
position of the branched chains and the length of the branched chains affect molecular packing? The
author needs to carefully analyze the molecular single crystal structure.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer for the insightful comment. To better explain how side-chain steric
hindrance affects the molecular packing in our work, we have analyzed the single-crystal data of NFAs
in a more in-depth manner and provided detailed explanations.
From the single-crystal analysis, S9SBH-F with the shortest N-alkyl chain forms an ordered 3D
honeycomb network, similar to the previously reported Y6 (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2020, 142, 15246-15251).
Compared with S9SBH-F, S9SHO-F with longer branched N-alkyl chains exhibits a long-range ordered
packing in the oblique direction across the crystal lattice (Supplementary Fig. 11), forming columns
composed of π-stacked NFA molecules with a small average π-π stacking distance (3.38 Å for S9SBH-
F, and 3.20 Å for S9SHO-F). The transition of crystal packing structure from a 3D honeycomb network
(S9SBH-F) into a network of rather independent columns (S9SHO-F) is caused by the long N-alkyl
chains occupying the interval between the adjacent columns in S9SHO-F single crystal, and results in
a mismatch between the two parallel molecules. When changing the branching site from C2-position to
C3-position, although the branching site of N-alkyls moves farther from the π-system, they still occupy
the interval between the adjacent molecular columns thus the packing patterns of S9S3B-F and S9SHN-
F are similar to that of S9SHO-F (Supplementary Fig. 12). We also infer that the distance between the
neighboring columns, which is associated with the size of N-alkyl substituents, may offer the flexibility
for NFA molecules to pack in a tighter manner. Therefore, we observe a reverse trend between the
distance in the neighboring columns (10.8 Å < 15.3 Å < 19.5 Å) and π-π stacking distance (3.52 Å >
3.50 Å > 3.20 Å) in S9S3B-F, S9SHN-F, and S9SHO-F (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 6).
To further investigate the π-π stacking in the neat NFAs, we conducted grazing-incidence wide-angle
X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) measurement of the C2-position and C3-position acceptors. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. 13, S9SHO-F shows a (010) diffraction peak at 1.76 Å-1 corresponding with a d-
spacing of 3.57 Å in the out-of-plane (OOP) direction. When changing the branching site to C3-position,
S9SHN-F exhibits a (010) diffraction peak at 1.73 Å-1 with a d-spacing of 3.63 Å in the OOP direction,
indicating a slightly more intimate packing in C2-position acceptor. These results are consistent with
our conclusions obtained from the single crystal analysis.

5. In most cases, selenium atom substitution results in the red shift of absorption, however, the inferior
PCEs (FFs) comparing to their sulfur counterparts, especially for 5Se acceptor with 5-selenium
substitution. What is the inner reason for that?
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer for the insightful comment. Selenium is more polarizable than sulfur,
and the lone pairs on selenium facilitates stronger interatomic interactions between adjacent selenium
atoms, resulting in enhanced intermolecular Se⋯Se interactions (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2015, 137, 1314;
Acc. Chem. Res. 2021, 54, 3906; Sol. RRL 2022, 6, 2200156). When introducing 5 selenium to the
design of small-molecule acceptors, it may induce excessively strong intermolecular Se⋯Se
interactions, leading to over-aggregation of the acceptor phase and inadequate miscibility between the
donor and acceptor, resulting in a non-ideal morphology. Therefore, the generation and transport of
charge carrier could be prohibited and leads to an inferior FF, as well as PCE.
